response.passage: To plot points on a Cartesian plane, we must always start from the origin, which is the intersection of the x-axis and y-axis at (0,0). When plotting the point (-2, 3), start at the origin and move 2 units to the left along the x-axis, then move 3 units up. It is vital to maintain equal spacing between numbers on your axes, regardless of where your data points fall, to ensure the graph is accurate. Once you have plotted several points for a linear relation, draw a straight line using a ruler that extends beyond the first and last points you marked. This line represents all possible solutions to the equation, not just the specific points you calculated. If you are tracking how a quantity like temperature changes over time, a line graph is the best choice, as it shows continuous trends. Avoid using pie charts for time-series data, as they are only meant to show parts of a whole at a single moment. Finally, remember that on a distance-time graph, a horizontal line indicates that the object is stationary, not moving at a constant speed.
response.summary: This guide explains how to correctly plot points on a Cartesian plane starting from the origin. It also highlights the importance of consistent axis scaling and using the right graph type for specific data. Finally, it clarifies how to interpret linear relations and distance-time graphs.
